title: Black Holes
summary: A comprehensive overview of black holes, examining their formation, anatomical structure, classification, and groundbreaking observational discoveries.
subject: Physics

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: Black holes are regions of spacetime where gravity is so intense that nothing, not even electromagnetic radiation such as light, possesses sufficient energy to escape. Predicted by Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity in 1915, they represent the ultimate gravitational consequence of concentrated mass. Shortly after Einstein published his field equations, Karl Schwarzschild derived the first exact solution describing a static, spherically symmetric black hole. Today, black holes have shifted from hypothetical mathematical oddities to confirmed, observable astrophysical objects that govern galactic evolution.

sections.heading: Anatomy and Core Mechanics
sections.body: The outer perimeter of a black hole is demarcated by the event horizon, a causal boundary where the local escape velocity equals the speed of light. Classical general relativity posits that all mass within the horizon collapses into an infinitely dense, zero-volume point known as a gravitational singularity. Surrounding many active black holes is an accretion disk, which consists of gas and plasma heated by friction and gravitational shear to millions of degrees Kelvin. In addition, rotating black holes can twist surrounding spacetime through frame-dragging and shoot relativistic particle jets thousands of light-years into space.

sections.heading: Observational Breakthroughs and Significance
sections.body: Because isolated black holes emit no detectable light, astronomers infer their existence by observing their gravitational influence on orbiting companion stars and surrounding gas clouds. In 2015, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) made the historic first direct detection of gravitational waves produced by two colliding stellar-mass black holes. Four years later, in 2019, the global Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) array captured the first resolved radio silhouette of the supermassive black hole at the center of the galaxy M87. These observational milestones offer physicists an unprecedented laboratory to test the boundaries of quantum mechanics and general relativity under extreme conditions.

keyTerms.definition: The theoretical boundary surrounding a black hole beyond which the escape velocity exceeds the speed of light.
A theoretical point in spacetime where matter is compressed to infinite density and standard laws of physics break down.
The radius that defines the event horizon for a non-rotating, spherically symmetric black hole of a given mass.
A rotating disk of superheated matter swirling toward a central gravitating body before crossing the event horizon.
Theoretical thermal radiation predicted to be emitted by black holes due to quantum vacuum fluctuations near the horizon.
